body.p: A procedure or function parameter can be declared byref so the caller passes a reference to the actual's storage rather than a value: the formal aliases the actual's bytes as a raw byte array, and the body re-types them with at overlays.
body.codeblock: procedure bump(byref in out arr[]) is var word v at arr v = v + 1 end procedure

section.title: Direction
section.p: byref is a type-position keyword with a direction: byref in arr[] (read-only), byref out arr[] (write-only) and byref in out arr[] (read-write). The direction is permission on the alias, not a copy-back: out and in out write the caller's storage immediately.

Any scalar, array or string actual converts to a byte view of its storage: a word is a 2-byte view, a dword or float a 4-byte view, a qword 8 bytes and an oword 16 bytes; an array is its total byte size. A string actual keeps its payload marshalling and stays element-accessible.

section.title: Type tag and predicates
section.p: Each byref formal carries one hidden runtime tag byte. Bits 0..2 are the size/type code: 0 byte, 1 word, 2 dword, 3 qword, 4 oword, 5 float. Bit 3 is string, bit 4 array, bit 5 pointer and bit 6 signed. An array carries its ELEMENT code plus ARRAY; a pointer carries its POINTEE code plus POINTER. A pointer-to-string actual is marshalled as a string and carries STRING only. The predicates lower to (tag & mask) == value, so a single-type call folds them to constants.
The predicates are built-in functions written _is_<type>(); the parentheses are optional. They return a bit and may only be used inside a procedure or function that has exactly one byref formal:
section.codeblock: procedure inspect(byref in v[]) is if _is_array() then out = 1 ; v is an array else if _is_sbyte() then out = 2 ; v is a signed byte end if end procedure
section.p: Any other use is refused with _is_*() needs exactly one byref formal in this procedure (found N).
Width predicates. The SIGNED bit is ignored, so _is_byte() is true for both byte and sbyte:
Signed predicates. These test the SIGNED bit, so they are true only for the explicitly signed type:
Kind predicates. These test what the actual is, not its element or pointee type:

row.entry: a dynamic string, or a pointer to a string
an array (including a fixed const byte[] = "...")

section.p: Element predicates. True for an array whose elements have the named type:
Pointee predicates. True for a pointer whose pointee has the named type:

A fixed const byte[] = "..." is an array, so it tests _is_array(), not _is_string(); a dynamic string and a pointer-to-string test _is_string(). When the procedure is re-flavored by pragma byref_clone, its formal is a string: inside that clone _is_string() is statically true and every other predicate is false.

section.title: No clone
section.p: A byref procedure compiles to ONE body regardless of the actual's type — the tag branches it instead of the compiler cloning it. pragma byref_clone on as the first line of a procedure opts that procedure back into the string-flavor clone. The clone's re-flavored formal is a string, so inside that clone _is_string() is true and the other predicates are false.
When every call site passes the same type, the compiler folds the tag and the predicates to constants and drops the dead branches, so the routine costs the same as a typed parameter.

ul.li: the old byte byref x modifier form is a clean error naming the type-position syntax;
a banked (chunked) array cannot be passed byref — the reference is linear and cannot walk the holes; pass an open array instead;
optional byref and byref formals in function-pointer signatures are refused;

a pointer actual may have a numeric or float pointee of any supported width (byte, word, dword, qword, oword, float); the hidden count is the pointee byte size and the pointer predicates report the pointee type. A pointer to a structure or another pointer is not a scalar view and is refused.
